citeAs: Pratap, V., Xu, Q., Sriram, A., Synnaeve, G., Collobert, R. (2020). MLS: A Large-Scale Multilingual Dataset for Speech Research. arXiv:2012.03411.
creator: Vineel Pratap, Qiantong Xu, Anuroop Sriram, Gabriel Synnaeve, Ronan Collobert (Facebook AI Research)
description: Multilingual LibriSpeech (MLS) is a large-scale multilingual speech dataset derived from read audiobooks from LibriVox, consisting of 8 languages including about 44.5K hours of English and a total of about 6K hours for other languages. The dataset is suitable for ASR and TTS research and is released freely under an open license. It also includes language models and baseline ASR models for all languages.
inLanguage: en, de, nl, fr, es, it, pt, pl
name: Multilingual LibriSpeech (MLS)
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: WER between generated transcript (GT) and human rated transcript (HRT) was measured for dev and test sets across all 8 languages. WER ranged from 1.93% (Spanish dev) to 12.64% (Portuguese dev), indicating the quality of automatically generated transcripts relative to human-verified ones.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Transcripts for development and test sets were human-verified: human transcribers listened to audio files while reading the generated transcript and were asked to correct only "clear and obvious" errors. For training data, transcripts were generated automatically via pseudo-label generation and transcript retrieval (TF-IDF + Smith-Waterman alignment).
rai:dataBiases: To avoid adding bias from human transcribing, transcribers were asked to only correct "clear and obvious" errors. The MLS development and test sets are chosen to be harder than LibriSpeech dev-/test-other partitions by selecting speakers with WER higher than 80% of those in dev-other sets.
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was collected by downloading audiobooks from LibriVox in 8 languages. Audio files were downsampled from 48kHz to 16kHz, segmented into 10-20 second segments, and matched to their original book transcripts via pseudo-label generation and TF-IDF/Smith-Waterman alignment. Text sources were downloaded from multiple domains including gutenberg.org, archive.org, ccel.org, and hathitrust.org, with some manual extraction for non-English languages.
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Some audiobook text sources had invalid links or were redirected to incorrect pages. For German, text sources from spiegel.de (accounting for 1/3 of German audio data) were being redirected to invalid pages; alternate sources were found manually. The training data is lower than raw LibriVox data because: (1) text source for some audiobooks was not downloaded, (2) candidate labels were filtered during transcript retrieval, or (3) filtered while creating valid/test splits.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Read audiobooks from LibriVox in 8 languages (English, German, Dutch, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Italian, Polish), along with corresponding book text sources from Project Gutenberg and other online domains. LibriVox provides audio files of varying duration (from a few minutes to hours).
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is read speech only (from audiobooks), which may limit applicability to spontaneous or conversational speech tasks. Polish has a very high OOV rate of 13.39% in the language model, which negatively impacts LM-based decoding. Some languages have significantly less data than English (e.g., Polish has only ~103 hours of training data). Some audiobook text sources were unavailable or had invalid links, limiting coverage.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Audio files were segmented into 10-20 second segments by splitting at the longest silence interval within the 10-20 second range. Dataset splits were created ensuring no speaker overlap between train/dev/test, with speakers balanced by gender and duration. Speakers with high duration in dev/test sets were truncated by sampling recordings up to an upper-bound. Limited supervision subsets (10h, 1h, 6x10min) were created by sampling from the training set.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Audio files were downsampled from 48kHz to 16kHz. Text was normalized using NFKC normalization, removal of punctuations, subscripts/superscripts, emojis, escape symbols, and end-of-line hyphens. Valid unicode characters were filtered based on language orthography. Numbers in text were replaced with aligned words from pseudo labels. Hyphens and apostrophes were handled with heuristics. Candidate transcripts with WER > 40% between pseudo label and candidate transcript were filtered out.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to promote open research in large-scale multilingual ASR and TTS. By providing a freely available multilingual corpus, it aims to democratize speech research across multiple languages, including languages that previously had limited open-license resources.
rai:dataUseCases: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) research, Text-To-Speech (TTS) research, multilingual ASR, low-resource speech research.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Acoustic models using Time-Depth Separable (TDS) Convolutions with Auto-Segmentation Criterion (ASG) loss were used for audio segmentation and pseudo-label generation. A 4-gram language model was used for beam-search decoding to generate pseudo labels. TF-IDF similarity on bigrams and Smith-Waterman alignment were used for transcript retrieval. A SVM gender classifier with RBF kernel was used to label speaker gender.

null_reasons.rai:annotationsPerItem: The paper does not specify a fixed number of annotations per item; training data uses automated transcripts and dev/test uses single human verification pass.
null_reasons.rai:annotatorDemographics: No demographic information about human transcribers/annotators is provided in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: The paper does not name a specific annotation platform used for human transcript verification.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: No specific timeframe for data collection is mentioned in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol for missing values is described; missing data was handled by finding alternate sources or filtering out records.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No versioning, update cadence, or maintenance plan is described in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset is derived from public domain audiobooks; no personal or sensitive information is discussed. In-house training data used for acoustic models is noted as de-identified but that is not part of the released dataset.

evidence.name: This paper introduces Multilingual LibriSpeech (MLS) dataset, a large multilingual corpus suitable for speech research.
evidence.description: This paper introduces Multilingual LibriSpeech (MLS) dataset, a large multilingual corpus suitable for speech research. The dataset is derived from read audiobooks from LibriVox and consists of 8 languages, including about 44.5K hours of English and a total of about 6K hours for other languages. Additionally, we provide Language Models (LM) and baseline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) models and for all the languages in our dataset.
evidence.url: The dataset will be made freely available for anyone at http://www.openslr.org .

evidence.inLanguage: Based on the number of audiobook hours and the availability of the corresponding text sources of the audiobooks, we have selected English, German, Dutch, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Italian, Polish for the MLS dataset preparation.
evidence.citeAs: Vineel Pratap, Qiantong Xu, Anuroop Sriram, Gabriel Synnaeve, Ronan Collobert Facebook AI Research, Menlo Park & Paris, USA & France
evidence.isLiveDataset: The dataset will be made freely available for anyone at http://www.openslr.org .
evidence.rai:dataCollection: For downloading the LibriVox audiobooks in these languages, we have used data preparation tools available at LibriLight open source library. All the audio data is downsampled from 48kHz to 16kHz for further processing.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The dataset is derived from read audiobooks from LibriVox and consists of 8 languages, including about 44.5K hours of English and a total of about 6K hours for other languages.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: For other languages, however, we found it more challenging to automatically extract text for the audiobooks... So, we have also incorporated some manual approaches in our process to cover the audiobook text sources as much as possible. Depending on the language and text source domain, we copied the text data directly from the browser or extracted text from .pdf/.epub books using pdftotext tool, or wrote HTML parsers to retrieve text data for popular domains in a language.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For normalizing the text, we first perform NFKC normalization and remove all the unwanted characters like punctuations, subscript/superscripts, emojis, escape symbols etc. We also remove the hyphens used for "end-of-line hyphenation" and join the parts of words into a single word. We then prepare a list of valid unicode characters based on the language's orthography and filter characters outside this range.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The human transcribers listen to the audio file while looking the transcript and are asked to correct the transcripts if they find any mistakes. To ensure that we do not add any potential bias into the dataset from human transcribing, we ask the transcribers to only correct "clear and obvious" errors.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Table 3: WER between generated transcript (GT) and human rated transcript (HRT). GT is considered as hypothesis and HRT as reference for measuring WER.
evidence.rai:machineAnnotationTools: We generate pseudo labels for the segmented audio samples by performing a beam-search decoding with a 4-gram language model on the same acoustic models used for audio segmentation... Second, we label the gender of all the speakers with a gender classifier. The classifier is a SVM with RBF kernel trained on 1172 speakers from train-clean-100 and train-clean-360 subsets of LibriSpeech.
evidence.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: We have used the following principles when splitting the dataset into train, development and test sets - 1) there is no speaker overlap between the training, development and test sets, 2) speakers are balanced in gender and duration in development and test sets and 3) there are sufficient audio hours and speakers assigned into development and test sets to be able to validate ASR model performance.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: We believe such a large transcribed dataset will open new avenues in ASR and Text-To-Speech (TTS) research... This dataset can also be used for Text-to-Speech (TTS) research by extending the LibriTTS dataset, and by creating a larger and multilingual version for TTS Research.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: To ensure that we do not add any potential bias into the dataset from human transcribing, we ask the transcribers to only correct "clear and obvious" errors.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: For Polish, the OOV rate is 13% as shown in Table 5 which negatively impacts the WER as we are performing LM decoding with constrained lexicon.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: We believe this dataset will promote open research in large-scale training of ASR systems and in multilingual ASR. This dataset can also be used for Text-to-Speech (TTS) research by extending the LibriTTS dataset, and by creating a larger and multilingual version for TTS Research.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: For the audiobooks with invalid links for text sources, we have also manually searched online to find alternate sources where the book is available. For example, all the text sources from the spiegel.de domain, which accounts of 1/3rd of German audio data, were being redirected to an invalid page.
